articles.title: After seeing patients lose their sight while waiting for treatment, Surat doctor Bhavin Patel takes eye care to Gujarat’s villages, with over 30,000 free surgeries and nearly 40 monthly screening camps
articles.summary: For some patients, the biggest barrier to saving their eyesight is not the treatment itself.
articles.body: For some patients, the biggest barrier to saving their eyesight is not the treatment itself. It is reaching a doctor before the condition becomes too serious. In parts of Gujarat, people living in remote villages may delay eye check-ups because of travel costs, limited awareness or difficulty accessing specialists. By the time they reach a hospital, a condition that could have been treated earlier may have already caused lasting damage.This is a problem that Dr Bhavin Patel, a retina specialist in Surat, has spent years trying to address. Instead of waiting for patients to find their way to a hospital, he has helped build an outreach system that takes eye screening into villages and brings patients who need treatment to Surat. According to figures shared in the original report by The Better India, the initiative has conducted more than 30,000 free surgeries and organises nearly 40 screening camps each month. Behind these numbers is an approach built around one simple idea: eye care must reach people before it is too late.The real problem begins before patients reach a hospitalDr Patel began his medical practice in Surat in 2008, starting with a clinic focused on retinal care. Over time, he encountered patients whose conditions had worsened because they could not access timely treatment. Some had ignored blurred vision, while others struggled to afford specialist consultations or travel to larger hospitals. For patients with serious retinal conditions, delays can have lasting consequences.The scale of preventable vision loss in India makes early diagnosis particularly important. A national survey conducted between 2015 and 2019 found that 92.9% of blindness and 97.4% of visual impairment among people aged 50 and above were attributable to avoidable causes. Cataract was responsible for 66.2% of blindness in this age group. The findings, published in PLOS ONE, underline the importance of accessible screening, timely treatment and follow-up care. For Dr Patel, the challenge was not simply to treat more patients. It was to identify people who needed help before their conditions became more difficult to manage.From village screenings to treatment in SuratThe outreach programme developed around Swami Vivekanand Netra Mandir, the eye hospital Dr Patel established in Surat. The associated non-profit trust was established in 2022, according to its official website. Its approach begins in villages, where local volunteers help identify residents who may need eye examinations. Screening teams check vision and look for signs of cataracts, retinal disorders and other eye conditions. People who need basic assistance, such as spectacles, can receive support through outreach services. Those who require surgery or specialist treatment are referred to the hospital in Surat. Transport is arranged for eligible patients, helping reduce the difficulties of travelling long distances.The programme also works with local community networks to encourage residents to attend screening camps. Familiar locations and trusted volunteers can make it easier for people to seek care, especially when they have limited information about eye diseases. According to the reported figures, the team conducts nearly 40 camps each month and around 1,000 free cataract surgeries monthly. The trust's official also lists community screening camps, school eye checks, spectacle distribution, treatment for premature babies with retinopathy of prematurity and vocational training for visually impaired people.When treatment restores more than eyesightThe impact of accessible eye care can extend beyond a medical outcome. For someone who depends on daily wages, poor vision can make earning a living difficult. For families, caring for a person who has lost their sight may also bring financial pressure and changes to everyday responsibilities. The original report by The Better India described the experience of Nathuram Makwana, a construction worker who lost vision in both eyes following a workplace injury. When he eventually received treatment, the improvement was limited, but even being able to perceive some light and shadows offered a measure of hope. His experience also encouraged him to advise others not to delay seeking medical help.Another case involved Vihana, a premature baby diagnosed with retinopathy of prematurity. Her family had already spent a substantial amount seeking treatment. After reaching Dr Patel's hospital, she underwent surgery on both eyes. Her father said the treatment brought relief to a family that had feared she might lose her sight. Such stories also highlight an important distinction: treatment cannot always restore vision completely. Outcomes depend on the condition, its severity and how early it is treated. That is why screening and timely referral remain essential.Building independence after vision lossDr Patel's work also addresses what happens when sight cannot be fully restored. Losing vision can affect a person's confidence, mobility, employment and ability to manage daily tasks independently. The trust's rehabilitation programme offers training in computer use, smartphone skills and mobility. The aim is to help visually impaired people build practical abilities and prepare for work rather than leaving them without support after treatment. This approach reflects a wider understanding of eye care. Medical treatment may address a condition, but rehabilitation can help people adapt, regain confidence and participate more independently in everyday life.The challenge of preventable blindness remains significant, particularly for people who struggle to reach healthcare services. By combining village screening, hospital treatment and rehabilitation, Dr Patel's initiative seeks to address several stages of that challenge. Its larger lesson is that healthcare cannot depend entirely on patients finding their way to specialists. Sometimes, the first and most important step is taking care closer to the communities that need it.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: A Dietitian’s ‘Perfect Fall Snack’ Is Packed With Plant Protein and Healthy Fats
articles.summary: Try this dietitian-approved recipe for a snack that’s packed with plant-based protein, fiber, omega-3s and more. Made with apple and spices, it’s a tasty treat.
articles.body: One of the most delicious ways to enjoy warm fall flavors is also one of the most nutritious. With plant-based protein, fiber and omega-3s, this dietitian-approved recipe is a tasty, energizing treat with major health benefits. This filling, energizing recipe is a favorite of Natalie Rizzo, registered dietitian and TODAY nutrition editor. She recommends grabbing some before a workout or as a sweet treat after a meal. Nutrition Tip of the Day: Try This No-Bake Fall Snack to Get More Plant-Based Protein Rizzo’s No-Bake Apple Spiced Energy Bites are a delicious autumnal snack that packs plant protein, fiber and more into a small, tasty package. “As a dietitian, I’m always looking for satisfying snacks that are easy to make and keep me full until my next meal,” she says. “These apple-spiced energy bites check all those boxes, and they’re the perfect fall snack.” In this snack, you’ll find oats, almond butter, apple chips, dates and delicious spices. But the starting ingredient is hemp seeds, Rizzo says, which are small but mighty. Why It Matters “Each bite offers a balance of nutrients,” Rizzo says. The oats provide complex carbohydrates and fiber, both of which support digestion and give you some lasting energy. “The almond butter adds plant-based protein and heart-healthy unsaturated fats,” she continues, “while the dates and dried apples provide natural sweetness and additional fiber.” Then there’s the hemp seeds, which provide more healthy fats and are a plant protein powerhouse. A 3-tablespoon serving of hemp seeds contains nearly 10 grams of protein, making them one of the top high-protein seeds. And a serving of Rizzo’s energy bites (3 pieces) will net you 7 grams of plant-based protein. Together, these nutrients will keep you feeling full, satisfied and energized. They’re perfect for a quick snack, an evening treat or a pre- or post-workout bite. How to Get Started To make Rizzo’s no-bake energy bites, you’ll just need a few ingredients, a food processor, a mixing bowl and a little patience. You’ll start by blitzing apple chips, oats, dates and almond butter in the food processor. Then you’ll add the hemp seeds and your spices to the mixture and form them into balls. The mixture comes together in about 10 minutes, and the energy bites will firm up after about an hour in the fridge. articles.title: Medieval hospital built for victims of feared disease gives up long-buried secrets
articles.summary: A three-day dig at Lincoln's Hospital of the Holy Innocents in England uncovered small structures that may have served as private quarters for leprosy patients.
articles.body: Archaeologists in England have uncovered new remains at one of the country's oldest and largest medieval leprosy hospitals, hundreds of years after the disease ravaged communities across Britain. The recent excavation, reported by British news agency Jam Press, centered on South Common in Lincoln, a historic English city roughly 140 miles north of London. The site was once home to the Hospital of the Holy Innocents, which was founded between the late 11th and early 12th centuries. MYSTERIOUS SETTLEMENT DISCOVERED AFTER RESIDENTS SEEMINGLY PACKED UP AND VANISHED During a three-day excavation, archaeologists from the British television program "Time Team" uncovered traces of medieval walls and possible living quarters. The hospital operated for nearly 500 years, housing up to 20 leprosy patients at a time, officials said. The findings build on an excavation that took place last year, when volunteers unearthed walls, building surfaces and artifacts linked to the former hospital. This time, researchers identified traces of small, square features that may have served as individual living quarters or enclosed yards for patients. The structures have never been excavated before, researchers said, according to Jam Press. SHOCKING DISCOVERY OF ANCIENT BONES TURNS COUPLE'S KITCHEN RENOVATION INTO 'CRIME SCENE' The findings offer a rare glimpse into how leprosy patients may have lived during the Middle Ages, including who could afford to receive care. "You'd need to have resources to get in here," professor Carenza Lewis of the University of Lincoln said, according to Jam Press. "If you had enough money and could buy your way into a leper hospital, it's a bit like getting a place in a private care home or something like that." Historical documents suggest the hospital accommodated up to 20 patients, who may have lived in separate structures with small yards, Lewis said. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER "We know that they had little sorts of curtilages [enclosed plots of land], which implies they're separate little buildings, little houses with a little yard, perhaps," she said. Leprosy, also known as Hansen's disease, is a chronic bacterial infection that primarily affects the skin, nerves and eyes. Although the disease can cause severe disfigurement if left untreated, it is curable with antibiotics and still exists today. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS The excavation is part of a three-year research project led by Anglia Ruskin University, which aims to learn more about the people who lived, worked and died at the medieval hospital. Leprosy is curable with antibiotics and still exists today. Tim Taylor, the creator of "Time Team," said the site could reveal more about Lincoln's archaeological past. The findings come after a similar discovery last year in York, England, where a sinkhole in a city street exposed the remains of one of northern England's largest medieval hospitals. articles.title: Matthew Perry’s Sister Says This Reframing Made it ‘Easier to Love Him’ Through Substance Use Disorder
articles.summary: Matthew Perry’s sister Mia Perry Bowick remembered him in a documentary and on TODAY and shared how she learned to understand his substance use disorder.
articles.body: Matthew Perry’s life is being remembered in a three-part documentary series by the people who knew him best, including his sister Mia Perry Bowick. “Yes, he was just that wonderful,” Bowick said during an appearance on TODAY Oct. 26. “All of those warm, comforting feelings you get from him, he gave them to his family and friends.” The “Friends” star died of acute effects of ketamine at 54 in October 2023. Perry had been open about his decadeslong struggle with addiction. He estimated in his memoir, which published one year before his death, that he spent $7 million on efforts to get sober. Bowick said in the documentary, out Oct. 27 on Netflix, that her brother’s struggle impacted her career path. She became a licensed psychotherapist working in substance use treatment. Bowick said when Perry first started telling people about addiction, there was “very little nuance or understanding about what substance use disorder is.” “I only had information from the D.A.R.E. program. It’s kind of very black and white — if you use a drug, you’re going to die,” she said. Bowick said she wished she understood at the time “it was a disease.” “When you can think of it from the disease perspective, it’s a lot easier to understand why they can’t stop, and it’s helpful for the families to not take it as personally that they can’t stop,” she said. “As we learned more and more about what’s happening to him, it was easier to love him through it, rather than try to control what was happening,” she added. Perry wrote in his memoir that he had a near death experience in 2019 after his colon burst from opioid overuse. He also said his heart stopped at a rehab facility in Switzerland. Perry had been receiving ketamine infusion therapy before his death “to ease pain and help with depression,” he wrote in his memoir. According to an autopsy, his last ketamine infusion therapy treatment had been a week and a half before his death, which could not have been the ketamine in his system when he died. Five individuals, including Perry’s assistant Kenneth Iwamasa and Jasveen Sangha, nicknamed the “Ketamine Queen, were charged in connection with Perry’s fatal drug overdose, per a press release from the U.S. Attorney’s Office, Central District of California. Prosecutors alleged their roles in distributing ketamine to Perry caused his death. Prosecutors said Perry was experiencing severe ketamine addiction and was injecting the drug six to eight times a day before his death. The actor sought out unsupervised doses and developed an “out of control” dependence on it, prosecutors said. If you or someone you know is struggling with an alcohol, drug or other substance use problem, call the free and confidential helpline of the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration at 1-800-662-HELP (1-800-662-4357), or visit findtreatment.gov.

articles.title: The No. 1 Anti-Inflammatory Plant-Based Protein, According to a Dietitian
articles.summary: Plant-based proteins come with all kinds of nutrients. These have anti-inflammatory benefits that support heart, gut and brain health, a dietitian says.
articles.body: Plant foods, including plant-based proteins, come with all kinds of nutrients. And that includes antioxidant and anti-inflammatory compounds that can benefit your heart, brain and gut health. “Inflammation is a normal part of the body’s immune response, but chronic inflammation is associated with conditions like cardiovascular disease and Type 2 diabetes,” explains Natalie Rizzo, registered dietitian and TODAY nutrition editor. “Eating anti-inflammatory foods regularly can reduce or eliminate chronic inflammation.” And the good news is that most plant-based proteins offer some of those anti-inflammatory compounds. “Antioxidants and polyphenols, unsaturated fats and fiber are all anti-inflammatory,” and can be found in many plant foods, Rizzo explains. Look for antioxidants because they help neutralize free radicals, unstable molecules that can damage cells, she says. Unsaturated fats are also useful because they “tend to replace pro-inflammatory saturated fats” in one’s diet, Rizzo says. And fiber “supports beneficial gut bacteria that produce compounds linked with lower inflammation,” she adds. Because there isn’t a single antioxidant or anti-inflammatory compound that does everything, Rizzo typically recommends people try to get a variety of these foods in their diet. Here are her favorite places to start. The Best Plant-Based Protein With Anti-Inflammatory Benefits Walnuts Rizzo previously crowned walnuts as the best plant-based protein to support brain health, so it’s not surprising they’re her top pick here as well. Walnuts provide about 4 grams of protein per 1-ounce serving, as well as 2 grams of fiber to support digestion and gut health. And they’re also full of antioxidants and alpha-linolenic acid (ALA), the essential plant-based omega-3 fatty acid. “Omega-3 fats are involved in regulating the body’s inflammatory processes,” Rizzo says. Research has shown that eating walnuts can have heart- and brain-health benefits, TODAY.com explained previously. These tasty nuts go great on oatmeal, yogurt and salads, and can make a delicious, filling snack on their own. Rizzo likes to roast them with a little maple syrup and cinnamon for a lightly sweet snack. Other Anti-inflammatory Plant Proteins to Try Edamame Edamame, which are immature green soybeans, pack 9 grams of protein and 4 grams of fiber into a single half-cup serving. “Soy is a complete plant protein and provides isoflavones, which have antioxidant and potentially anti-inflammatory properties,” Rizzo explains. You can also get those isoflavones in other soy foods, like tofu and soy milk. But edamame have the added benefit of gut-healthy fiber. Try adding edamame to noodles and stir fries, or take Rizzo’s cue to roast them with savory seasonings for a crispy snack. Chia Seeds When you’re looking for more heart-healthy unsaturated fats, reach for seeds. In particular, chia seeds are among the seeds with the most anti-inflammatory ALAs, TODAY.com explained previously. They’re also full of fiber: A 2-tablespoon serving of chia seeds will net you 10 grams of fiber alongside 5 grams of filling protein. Rizzo also recommends hemp seeds, which are similarly high in ALAs. Where chia seeds excel in fiber, hemp seeds are winners in protein. A serving of hemp seeds (3 tablespoons) packs in 10 grams of plant-based protein. Choose the seeds that you prefer and that work with the meal you’re making. For instance, sprinkle hemp seeds on smoothies or use them in baking. Meanwhile, chia seeds are great mixed in with overnight oats, or use them to make chia seed pudding with fresh fruit.

articles.title: ‘Looney Tunes’ Actor Eric Bauza’s Cause of Death, Explained
articles.summary: A day after Eric Bauza’s family announced the voice actor’s shocking death at the age of 46, the Los Angeles Medical Examiner has confirmed his cause of death.
articles.body: A day after Eric Bauza’s family announced the voice actor’s shocking death at the age of 46, the Los Angeles Medical Examiner has confirmed his cause of death. Records on the medical examiner’s website list Bauza’s cause of death as hypertensive cardiovascular disease. The medical examiner also included sleep apnea and obesity as “other significant conditions” that played a role in his death. Bauza died on Sunday, Oct. 25, in his residence, according to the records. The manner of death was determined to be “natural.” The death of the voice actor, who voiced “Looney Tunes” characters Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck, Porky Pig and more, was announced by his family in a brief statement shared on his Instagram page Oct. 25. He was 46. “Eric Bauza, Emmy Award-winning voice actor and the modern voice of iconic Looney Tunes characters Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck, along with dozens of other beloved cartoon characters, has passed away suddenly. More details to come,” the statement read. The Canadian-American won three Emmys for voicing beloved characters like Elmer Fudd, Marvin the Martian and Tweety. He also made history as the first person of color to voice Bugs Bunny in the “Looney Tunes” cartoons. During an interview with NBC News in 2021, Bauza spoke about the bond the characters created between his Filipino immigrant father and his grandfather. “I hope to make him proud with all this work,” he said, referencing his grandfather, whom he never met. “‘Looney Tunes’ transcends all languages and all cultures,” he added. “There are some cartoons that don’t even have English-speaking parts in it. There are some ‘Looney Tunes’ cartoons that are pantomimes. It doesn’t matter what part of the planet you’re from. You get the comedy.” What Was Eric Bauza’s Cause of Death? Hypertensive heart disease is a condition that causes damage to the heart after “years of unmanaged or under-managed high blood pressure,” according to the Cleveland Clinic. The disease can lead to a thick and weak heart muscle or heart failure. “Hypertensive heart disease is the No. 1 cause of illness and death due to high blood pressure,” according to the clinic. Sleep apnea is a condition that causes people to stop breathing while they are sleeping. The clinic notes that sleep apnea “can also put stress on your heart that may be life-threatening if untreated.” Obesity can lead to other serious medical conditions, as well, such as cardiovascular diseases, fatty liver disease, gallstones, kidney disease and Type 2 diabetes, the clinic says. Sleep apnea is one of the possible effects obesity has on the body.

articles.title: As More Young People Suffer Strokes, 29-Year-Old Recalls Early Signs: ‘A Bomb Went Off in My Head’
articles.summary: In July 2024, Patrick Mascoli, 29, of Boston, had just finished an ordinary run when something felt terribly wrong.
articles.body: In July 2024, Patrick Mascoli, 29, of Boston, had just finished an ordinary run when something felt terribly wrong. He was in the gym’s changing room when he suddenly felt an intense, burning pain on the right side of his head. The room began spinning, his vision blurred and he struggled to control his limbs. “It felt like a bomb went off in my head,” Mascoli recalls. He began vomiting and sweating profusely, and he couldn’t move. “I tried to take a step with my right leg. And instead of going forward, it went completely to the right, and I just slid down the wall and fell to the ground.” Unable to control his body, he tried to crawl in search of help. Eventually, he managed to call his sister, who came to the gym and found him unable to speak or move. She called emergency medical services, and paramedics took Mascoli to the hospital. At first, emergency medical personnel thought Mascoli might be severely dehydrated. When his dizziness and vomiting continued, they considered vertigo. But after he was transferred to Boston Medical Center for further testing, an MRI revealed that he had suffered a stroke in his right cerebellum, the part of the brain that helps control balance, coordination and movement. “I was shocked,” he says. “I didn’t make the connection that this is something that can happen when you’re 27 … without some pre-existing condition.” A Stroke in a Healthy, Active 27-Year-Old According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the leading causes of stroke are high blood pressure, high cholesterol, smoking, obesity and diabetes. But Mascoli was a healthy, active 27-year-old without any of those conditions, leaving doctors searching for answers. Testing later revealed that Mascoli had a patent foramen ovale (PFO), a small opening between the heart’s upper chambers that is present in some people from birth. According to the American Heart Association, a PFO affects roughly one in four adults, and many people never know they have one. In some cases, a PFO can allow a blood clot to pass from the right side of the heart to the left and travel to the brain. However, doctors could not definitively determine whether Mascoli’s PFO caused his stroke. About a month after the stroke, Mascoli underwent a procedure to close the opening in the heart. Doctors inserted a closure device, called an occluder, through a vein and guided it to his heart. The device helps seal the opening. He spent about a week in the hospital. At first, even walking was difficult, but he was able to walk to the bathroom about three days after the surgery. Some movements improved quickly, while others — particularly those on his right side — took longer to resolve. The most frightening part for Mascoli was that he didn’t know what his recovery might look like. “The doctors didn’t know exactly what the effects (of the stroke) would be. That was scary because, at that point, I couldn’t really walk. I couldn’t hold a fork with my hand,” he says. “I was like, ‘What is this going to look like a week from now, a month from now, 10 years from now?’” He says he was internally panicking and trying not to show it to his family. “I always want to be there for them and help them,” he says. “For once, I needed their help.” Stroke Rates Rising Among Young Adults Mascoli’s experience appears to be part of a research-backed trend. A 2026 study published in the journal Neurology found that the rate of stroke among adults ages 20-54 nearly doubled between 1993 and 2020, while rates declined in older adults. The increase was largely driven by ischemic strokes, which occur when a blood clot blocks blood flow to part of the brain. Researchers also found that high blood pressure, diabetes, atrial fibrillation and substance use were more common among younger adults who had strokes in the later years of the study. However, the study could not establish what caused the increase in stroke rates. Because the research focused on one region of the United States, its findings do not provide a precise estimate of national stroke risk. Mascoli’s case also illustrates that there isn’t always a clear explanation for why a stroke happens. Although doctors discovered a PFO, they could not definitively link it to his stroke. Returning to Running After a Stroke After leaving the hospital, Patrick began rebuilding his strength and coordination. He returned to work after about a month and practiced fine motor skills through activities such as playing video games, writing, drawing and solving puzzles. “My right side just always felt like it was lagging behind, or it was a little unstable,” he says. “Slowly, it did come back.” When he returned to work, he noticed that his handwriting had become shaky. “My hand still shakes a little bit and has a little bit of tremor. Specifically if I’m tired, I notice it,” he says. Mascoli avoided exercise until two months after his PFO closure and recovery. When he finally started running again, he kept it short, sometimes running for just 10 minutes or sticking to a one-mile route. “It just took time,” he says. He gradually increased his distance and frequency, but it took about six months to get close to his previous running level. ‘I Just Bawled My Eyes Out’ In October 2026, Mascoli ran the Chicago Marathon as part of Team Abbott, a group of runners who have overcome health challenges. Abbott also manufactures the occluder used to close the opening in his heart. The marathon represented more than a race for Mascoli. It was a milestone in a recovery that had once felt uncertain. “I just bawled my eyes out when I crossed the finish line,” he says. “It just meant a lot to me.” The experience also changed what Mascoli values about running. Before his stroke, he might have focused more on getting faster or completing a challenging workout. Now, he finds meaning in the everyday moments he once took for granted. Mascoli takes daily aspirin and a statin, and he continues to manage the anxiety that can linger even when physical recovery is going well. He still worries about why the stroke happened and whether he could experience another complication. “I still get anxious,” he says, especially since doctors haven’t determined the cause. Mascoli is also participating in a stroke study and has met other people who have experienced strokes, many of whom are much older than he is. The experience has helped him appreciate how far he has come, even as he continues to work through lingering symptoms and worries. Completing the Chicago Marathon gave him a chance to recognize his progress and celebrate the life he has been able to return to. “I’m very grateful for where I’m at,” he says.

articles.title: ROBERT F KENNEDY JR, DR MEHMET OZ: 250 hospitals join the fight for healthier food
articles.summary: Over 250 hospitals joined the Make Hospital Food Healthier Pledge to cut processed food and added sugar from patient meals under Trump's health agenda.
articles.body: When Americans enter a hospital, they expect to receive care that helps them heal. They trust their doctors, nurses and other healthcare professionals to provide the best possible treatments and give them the greatest chance of recovery. Yet too often, the food our nation’s hospitals serve contradicts that mission. Patients recovering from surgery, living with chronic diseases or managing serious medical conditions may be served hospital meals featuring highly processed foods, refined carbohydrates, added sugars and other ingredients that do little to support their recovery. RFK JR HAILS FIRST US HOSPITAL TO PROMISE HEALTHIER MEALS: 'WE HAVE A TEMPLATE' It’s a contradiction that should concern every American. And it’s one we’re determined to change. Today, we announce that 250 hospitals across the United States have joined the Make Hospital Food Healthier Pledge, a nationwide initiative the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) launched to improve the nutritional quality of meals that hospitals serve to patients and staff. AOC SAYS MAHA ADVOCATES' FIGHT 'ISN'T PARTISAN' AS SHE BLASTS HEALTHCARE SYSTEM FOR FUELING 'A TON OF ANXIETY' These commitments reflect a growing recognition among America’s healthcare leaders that food is an essential part of good medicine, and hospitals should demonstrate that through the meals they serve. Under President Donald Trump’s leadership, the Make America Healthy Again movement is fundamentally rethinking the role of nutrition in American healthcare. But transforming American healthcare requires more than changing federal policies; it requires changing the environments in which Americans receive care. Hospitals can help change those environments. They care for our most vulnerable citizens, educate millions of patients and families, and earn their communities’ trust. Nutrition is central to each of these responsibilities. For patients recovering from surgery, fighting infections or managing chronic illnesses, proper nutrition can support wound healing, preserve muscle mass, strengthen immune function and improve recovery. Malnutrition, by contrast, correlates with longer hospital stays, more complications and greater healthcare costs. THIS AMOUNT OF DELI MEAT ASSOCIATED WITH HIGHER DEMENTIA RISK IN COMPELLING NEW REVIEW Hospitals also have an opportunity to teach patients habits that can improve their health long after discharge. Consider a patient who enters the hospital for complications of Type 2 diabetes. That patient may receive excellent medical treatment and counseling about the importance of healthy eating. But if the meals the hospital serves during their stay contradict that advice, what message are we sending? A hospital meal should reinforce the care plan, not undermine it. There are approximately 6,100 hospitals in the United States, collectively accounting for more than 35 million hospital admissions each year. The broader American healthcare foodservice market represents nearly $20 billion in annual economic activity. That’s extraordinary purchasing power. Hospitals are among the largest customers of major foodservice management companies, food distributors and manufacturers. Their purchasing decisions influence which products suppliers develop, how suppliers price those products and what becomes available to other institutions. Imagine what could happen if hospitals across America began sending a consistent message to their suppliers: We want more real food. We want healthier proteins, fruits, vegetables and minimally processed ingredients. We want fewer products with added sugars and unnecessary additives. The food industry would have a powerful incentive to respond. As demand grows, suppliers can expand production, improve distribution networks and invest in healthier product offerings. Larger purchasing volumes and more predictable demand can also create economies of scale, potentially reducing costs and making nutritious food more affordable. Other institutions could also benefit. The same foodservice companies supplying hospitals often serve schools, universities, workplaces and other institutions. Improvements in their product offerings and supply chains could help make healthier food more accessible throughout American society. Hospitals could improve their patients’ health and help transform the nation’s food system. With more than 250 hospitals now participating, we’re beginning to demonstrate what healthcare institutions can accomplish together. We recognize that hospitals face real operational challenges. Hospital supply chains are complex, and patients have diverse medical and nutritional needs. That’s why the Make Hospital Food Healthier Pledge is voluntary and collaborative. We are not interested in Washington dictating hospital menus or second-guessing the clinical judgment of physicians and registered dietitians. Hospitals must retain the flexibility to meet patients’ individual nutritional requirements, including those who need specialized therapeutic diets or medical nutrition support. Our goal is to get hospitals across the country to improve the nutritional quality of their meals together. We are grateful for the partnership of the American Hospital Association and the many healthcare systems that have joined this effort. Their leadership demonstrates that change does not always require new mandates, complicated regulations or additional administrative burdens. Sometimes, it begins with a shared commitment. Hospitals should be places where every aspect of the patient experience supports health and healing. The food hospitals serve on a patient’s tray should support that goal. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Two hundred and fifty hospitals have already committed to serving healthier food. Now, we’re calling on the rest of America’s hospitals to join them. Mehmet Oz, M.D., M.B.A., is the administrator of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services.

articles.title: New test could flag which men need aggressive prostate cancer treatment and which don't
articles.summary: The Decipher genomic test could help doctors decide which high-risk prostate cancer patients need abiraterone hormone therapy and which can skip it.
articles.body: A new diagnostic test could improve the prostate cancer experience for millions of men. Researchers at University College London (UCL) analyzed a tissue-based molecular test called Decipher to determine which men with high-risk prostate cancer were most likely to benefit from stronger treatment — and which might avoid unnecessary medication and side effects. The analysis focused on abiraterone, a hormone therapy that was shown in the STAMPEDE clinical trial to cut the risk of death in half among men with high-risk, localized prostate cancer. The findings were presented at the European Society for Medical Oncology (ESMO) Congress 2026 in Madrid, held Oct. 23–27. JOE BIDEN SHARES HEALTH UPDATE AFTER PROSTATE CANCER DIAGNOSIS WHILE ISSUING WARNING TO OTHERS Not every cancer is alike, and treating someone more aggressively than necessary could have "increased side effects and poorer quality of life," noted a UCL news release. Because prostate cancers differ at the molecular level, not every patient benefits from adding hormone therapy. To determine whether Decipher could help guide that decision, researchers examined test scores from more than 27,000 patients in real-world data and 401 men with non-metastatic prostate cancer who had participated in the STAMPEDE abiraterone trial. PATIENTS REMAIN CANCER-FREE NEARLY 3 YEARS AFTER RECEIVING EXPERIMENTAL IMMUNOTHERAPY Higher Decipher scores predicted worse outcomes, meaning the cancer is more likely to spread and additional treatment may be valuable. A low Decipher score suggested more intensive treatment may be unnecessary. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Lead researcher Dr. Sarah Howlett of UCL Cancer Institute commented in a statement that for men with very high-risk prostate cancer, preventing spread of the disease is "critical." "Understanding who benefits most from additional treatment can make a meaningful difference," she added. The findings suggest that genomic testing could help tailor treatment, according to the researcher. Men with high-risk prostate cancer and low Decipher scores may face a lower risk of spread and could avoid more intensive therapy, while those with high scores may be the strongest candidates for additional treatment. Identifying the same pattern in both a large, real-world dataset and a randomized clinical trial strengthens the findings, Howlett noted. CANCER WARNING SIGNS MAY APPEAR IN DNA YEARS BEFORE BLOOD TESTS DETECT TROUBLE "But further validation in other datasets is needed before the test is used routinely to make these decisions," she said. Elai Davicioni, medical director of urology for Decipher test maker Veracyte, also commented, "We believe this growing evidence gives physicians a stronger reason to use Decipher before making decisions that can affect both cancer outcomes and patients’ quality of life." Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel, who was not involved in the study, also commented on the findings. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES "Prostate cancer varies from person to person," he said. "Medical science is increasingly aware that it is not one size fits all." Localized prostate cancer, which has not yet spread, may contain mutations that predict how aggressive the disease will be and indicate whether it could respond to targeted therapies, Siegel noted. Certain targeted therapies are being used more with widespread prostate cancer, according to the doctor, as they include "more powerful anti-androgens, which works not just on the testes, but on the adrenals as well." Hormone therapies have "significant side effects," including fatigue, and "don’t always help," he added. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Siegel said the study’s strength was its combination of a randomized treatment group with Decipher testing, which helped identify in advance which patients were most likely to respond to intensive hormone therapy. "This is the personalized, precise approach of the near future," he said. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER Prostate cancer is the second-leading cause of cancer death behind lung cancer, according to the American Cancer Society. About one in eight American men will be diagnosed with prostate cancer in their lifetime.

articles.title: Gavião é usado para afastar pombos de hospital em Vitória | G1
articles.standfirst: Shiluba, macho de 6 anos e cerca de 500 gramas, sobrevoa áreas externas do Hospital Universitário para afastar as aves. Trabalho usa o instinto natural do predador e busca reduzir riscos à saúde.
articles.summary: Shiluba, macho de 6 anos e 500 gramas, sobrevoa áreas externas do Hospital Universitário para afastar aves. Trabalho usa o instinto natural do predador para reduzir riscos à saúde
articles.body:
Gavião Shiluba é utilizado para afastar pombos de área de hospital do Espírito Santo — Foto: Divulgação/Hucam

Há cerca de quatro meses, o Hospital Universitário Cassiano Antônio Moraes (Hucam), em Vitória , passou a contar com o trabalho de um novo "funcionário". Shiluba, um gavião macho da espécie asa-de-telha (Parabuteo unicinctus), sobrevoa áreas externas da unidade para espantar pombos que encontram abrigo nos telhados, beirais e outras estruturas do hospital.

O projeto foi motivado depois que a administração do hospital percebeu o aumento da população de pombos na área da unidade, que fica no bairro Maruípe. Um censo da população na área apontou a presença de cerca de 60 pombos no entorno do hospital.

A presença de pombos em áreas próximas a hospitais preocupa, já que as fezes das aves podem favorecer a exposição a fungos, bactérias e parasitas, além de provocar danos a estruturas e sistemas de ventilação e ar-condicionado, expondo uma população que já está vulnerável.

Apesar dos riscos, o hospital não registrou casos de doenças transmitidas por pombos na unidade . A iniciativa tem caráter preventivo e busca reduzir a presença das aves antes que ela se torne um problema.

Hospital Universitário Cassiano Antônio Moraes (Hucam), em Vitória, Espírito Santo — Foto: Divulgação/Hucam

A unidade vinha adotando medidas convencionais como fechar pontos de entrada e promover ações de conscientização, mas elas não foram suficientes para resolver a situação.

"A estrutura do Hucam é um dos fatores que favorecem a presença dos pombos. Os prédios estão distribuídos horizontalmente, por uma área com desníveis e oferecem diversos pontos de abrigo, como telhados, beirais e janelas. A unidade já havia tentado fechar pontos de entrada, o uso de repelentes e promover ações de conscientização da comunidade, mas nada havia sido tão efetivo", explicou o biólogo David Salles, responsável pelo controle ambiental do Hucam.

O trabalho que começou a ser feito com o gavião é realizado por uma empresa especializada em falcoaria , técnica que utiliza aves de rapina treinadas para afastar outras espécies.

Shiluba é um macho de 6 anos que também atua no Aeroporto de Vitória realizando o mesmo serviço, só que neste caso, faz as rondas com outras três aves.

Além do senso para estimar o número de pombos no local, o trabalho no hospital começou com um mapeamento da área e a definição de rotas de voo.

De acordo com Gabriel Furtado, médico-veterinário e coordenador do projeto de falcoaria no Hucam, a estratégia se baseia na relação natural entre predador e presa.

"É uma relação presa e predador mesmo. A espécie é um predador natural de pombos, o próprio animal entende aquilo como uma ameaça", explica.

As rondas são realizadas preferencialmente no início da manhã, quando os pombos começam a sair dos abrigos para procurar alimento e estão menos ativos. Nesse horário, a circulação de pessoas no hospital também costuma ser menor. Dependendo da necessidade, o trabalho pode ocorrer à tarde.

O trabalho começou semanalmente e agora já passou a ser quinzenal. Segundo David, a diminuição da população de pombos já pode ser percebida.

"Já deu pra perceber que a quantidade diminuiu, foi mais rápido do que esperávamos. Agora, um novo censo está em andamento para reavaliar o tamanho dessa população e ajudar a definir a frequência das ações", disse o servidor do hospital.

Gavião Shiluba é utilizado para afastar pombos de área de hospital do Espírito Santo — Foto: TV Gazeta

Para que Shiluba consiga voar com eficiência e responda aos estímulos durante o trabalho, a preparação exige treinamento, alimentação controlada e acompanhamento diário.

O peso ideal de voo dessa ave gavião é de aproximadamente 500 gramas . Antes das atividades, Shiluba é pesado pela equipe, que calcula a quantidade de alimento necessária com base no gasto de energia previsto para a rotina.

O controle é importante porque o peso interfere diretamente no desempenho do animal. Se estiver muito leve, o gavião pode ter dificuldade para controlar o voo. Se estiver pesado demais, pode perder o interesse necessário para responder aos estímulos do treinamento.

A escolha da espécie também é importante para evitar impactos sobre outras aves. Segundo Gabriel, o gavião não costuma demonstrar interesse por pássaros menores, e algumas dessas espécies nem sequer se assustam com sua presença.

"Por isso, a falcoaria é considerada uma alternativa de baixo impacto ambiental para afastar aves de locais onde elas podem causar problemas. A técnica é utilizada em aeroportos de diferentes países, além de hospitais, galpões e plantas industriais", apontou Gabriel.

A empresa responsável pelo serviço no Hucam também atua no Aeroporto de Vitória, onde trabalha com quatro aves e realiza as ações com maior frequência. A companhia tem matriz em Belo Horizonte, Minas Gerais, e presta serviços no Espírito Santo e em outros estados.

De acordo com David, as fezes dos pombos podem favorecer a exposição a fungos, bactérias e parasitas, além de provocar danos a estruturas e sistemas de ventilação e ar-condicionado.

Entre as doenças associadas aos pombos estão a criptococose, que pode afetar os pulmões e, em casos graves, atingir o sistema nervoso central; a salmonelose, uma infecção gastrointestinal; e a histoplasmose, uma infecção fúngica sistêmica causada pela inalação de esporos do fungo Histoplasma capsulatum.

A histoplasmose, inclusive, foi confirmada pela Secretaria de Estado da Saúde (Sesa) e pela Fiocruz como a causadora de surto de contaminação no hospital Hospital Santa Rita , também na capital, há um ano.

A atuação do gavião faz parte de uma estratégia mais ampla de controle ambiental. David destaca que a participação de pacientes, funcionários e visitantes é importante para evitar que os pombos continuem encontrando alimento no local. São feitas também ações de sensibilização com esses grupos, apresentando o Shiluba e explicando o trabalho que está sendo feito na área da unidade.

"Não alimentar os pombos é uma das principais orientações da equipe. O descarte correto de restos de comida, o uso das lixeiras e o cuidado para não deixar alimentos expostos também ajudam a tornar o ambiente menos atrativo para as aves", apontou o biólogo.

A equipe orienta ainda que ninguém tente tocar em Shiluba durante as atividades e que as instruções dos profissionais sejam respeitadas.

articles.title: Diego Gonzaga: quem era o trabalhador morto em máquina de gelo? | G1
articles.standfirst: Diego Fernando Gonzaga, de 39 anos, tinha uma filha de 19 e trabalhava havia duas décadas na indústria de alimentos em Santa Luzia. Família o descreve como alegre e extrovertido.
articles.summary: Diego Gonzaga trabalhava há 20 anos na indústria de alimentos e deixa uma filha. Família descreve a trajetória do trabalhador morto em acidente em Santa Luzia.
articles.body:
Diego Gonzaga, trabalhador que morreu em máquina de triturar gelo, era morador de Santa Luzia, na Grande BH — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo

Pai de uma jovem de 19 anos, Diego Fernando Gonzaga, de 39, era conhecido na família pelo jeito alegre, falante e extrovertido. Morador de Santa Luzia, na Grande BH, desde que nasceu, ele morreu nesta segunda-feira (26), após ficar preso em uma máquina de triturar gelo no frigorífico onde trabalhava .

Segundo a prima Mariana Alberto, Diego gostava de cantar e dançar e demonstrava vontade de aproveitar a vida.

“Ele era muito alegre e sempre vivia cantando e dançando. Ele queria viver, viver intensamente, ser feliz”, contou.

Diego trabalhava havia dois anos no setor de embalagens da empresa onde ocorreu o acidente. Antes, passou 18 anos em outra indústria de alimentos, também em Santa Luzia, de acordo com a prima.

Para Mariana, o jeito de se comunicar e de conviver com as pessoas era uma das marcas dele.

“Ele era único, falante, extrovertido”, afirmou.

A prima também contou que a mãe de Diego estava muito abalada com a morte do filho.

“A ficha não caiu. Está muito sentida”, disse.

O acidente aconteceu no frigorífico HG Foods, antigo Frial, no bairro Fazenda. Segundo o registro policial, Diego caiu dentro da máquina de triturar gelo, na parte superior do equipamento.

O Corpo de Bombeiros foi acionado por volta das 8h. Os militares usaram equipamentos hidráulicos e ferramentas de corte para retirar o trabalhador, com apoio de equipes do Serviço de Atendimento Móvel de Urgência (Samu).

Durante o resgate, Diego sofreu uma parada cardiorrespiratória. As equipes fizeram manobras de reanimação, mas ele não resistiu e morreu no local.

A perícia foi realizada, e o corpo foi encaminhado ao Instituto Médico-Legal (IML), conforme o registro policial. As circunstâncias da queda não foram detalhadas no documento.

O g1 entrou em contato com a empresa em que ocorreu o acidente, mas, até o momento da publicação desta reportagem, não obteve retorno.

Mariana afirmou que, até o momento da entrevista, a empresa não havia entrado em contato com a família. Segundo ela, a ajuda recebida até então estava relacionada à funerária.

“A empresa ainda não entrou em contato. A única coisa foi a questão da funerária que prestava ajuda”, disse.

articles.title: Daisy Hill: 'What does it say if a woman can't give birth in her own city?'
articles.summary: The Southern Health Trust plans to temporarily transfer inpatient maternity services from Daisy Hill to Craigavon.
articles.body:
A woman who was rushed 40 miles (64km) to a maternity unit after going into premature labour says her experience shows why services must remain at her local hospital.

Because she required specialist care, midwives at Daisy Hill in Newry wanted to send Natasha Daryaie to Craigavon Area Hospital but were told there was no room.

The Southern Health Trust plans to temporarily transfer inpatient maternity services from Daisy Hill to Craigavon because it has been unable to recruit enough consultant obstetricians to safely staff both hospitals.

A spokesperson for the trust said that, following operational and workforce assessments, inpatient maternity care at Craigavon had been identified as the safest and most sustainable arrangement for maintaining services.

The trust says it is continuing efforts to recruit consultant obstetricians for Daisy Hill while preparing to temporarily consolidate births and inpatient maternity care at Craigavon from 23 November.

However, mothers in the Newry area say losing local inpatient maternity services would leave families facing longer journeys at a time when they may need urgent care.

"The journey was scary. I was having contractions every five minutes but a midwife from Daisy Hill travelled with me to the Ulster Hospital where I spent four nights, was stabilised and then sent home," Natasha said.

"What does it say if a woman can't give birth in her own city?"

The trust has five vacant obstetrician posts and said it cannot provide a safe maternity service at Daisy Hill without the required medical cover.

Its chief executive Steve Spoerry told Stormont's Health Committee that keeping women and babies safe was its highest priority.

He said the trust would not have enough consultants to staff both maternity units' daytime and out-of-hours rotas, adding that a transfer of services to Craigavon is "highly probable" from next month.

Natasha, whose son Odin was eventually born at Daisy Hill at full term, said her experience showed why having services close to home mattered particularly in rural areas which she believes should be treated differently.

"It's all well and good saying Craigavon is there but they didn't have room for me that night - that is the reality: Craigavon did not have room for one local mum from Newry," Natasha said.

"How are they going to accommodate 1,400 babies and mums in the future?"

Another mother, Seanan Martin, said removing a service was not the answer and that the safety of mothers, babies and staff should be the priority.

She said the workforce challenges should have been planned for years in advance.

Midwifery numbers fall at both hospitals

The number of midwives employed in the acute maternity units at Daisy Hill and Craigavon has fallen since October 2019.

The trust says the way midwifery care is delivered has changed, with more midwives now working in the community.

The figures show the number of full-time midwives employed at the two hospitals.

The current vacancies equate to 0.61 full-time posts at Daisy Hill and 11.69 at Craigavon.

The trust says 16 newly appointed midwives are due to start between November 2026 and January 2027.

It employs 15 consultant obstetricians but says sickness, reduced working arrangements and maternity leave mean not all are available for the consultant on-call rota.

The trust says staffing levels remain below what is required to fully staff both maternity units.

How will Craigavon cope with more births?

The number of babies born at Daisy Hill increased between 2019 and 2025, while births at Craigavon fell.

Dale Spence, the director of the Royal College of Midwives in Northern Ireland, said to provide the care that women deserve, more midwives were required and that those who are working are feeling overburdened.

Speaking publicly for the first time about the present condition of maternity services, she added that Northern Ireland should not be relying on the goodwill of midwives to keep some services afloat.

Midwives are doing the best they can to provide care for mothers and their babies, Spence said, but the system is under so much pressure that it feels like they are working with their hands tied behind their back.

The trust has been asked how Craigavon will manage approximately 1,400 additional births each year if inpatient maternity services move from Daisy Hill.

It says it is continuing to seek consultant obstetricians for Daisy Hill while preparing continuity arrangements to consolidate births and inpatient maternity care at Craigavon temporarily.

The trust has also acknowledged that, following the withdrawal of emergency general surgery from Daisy Hill in 2024, maternity services introduced a risk-stratification standard operating procedure to support the safe delivery of care.

This means fewer women have been considered suitable for elective Caesarean sections at Daisy Hill, which has had a subsequent decline in overall birth numbers over the past two years.

Other families are concerned about how Craigavon will cope with the additional births.

That includes Mark and Naomi Annett whose third child, a daughter, was born last Thursday.

They live in Kilkeel, County Down, and the journey to Daisy Hill takes about 35 minutes, depending on the time of day. Travelling to Craigavon would add another hour.

"With my wife's second birth it was minutes from when her waters broke to when the baby was born - thankfully we were already in the hospital," he said.

"I don't think we would have made it to Daisy Hill from home, never mind Craigavon.

"My fear would be what would happen to my wife and our baby if it was born halfway to Craigavon and us going over the mountains."

Mark thinks that "geography really matters" when it comes to health care.

"Craigavon could have the best maternity care on the planet but it doesn't matter if you can't get there on time," he said.

"Babies aren't good timekeepers, they can come early, late and with so many issues around a birth it does mean lives are in danger.

"It's not trying to scare monger people, it is reality."

articles.title: ‘Big Brother’ Season 28 Winner Rick Devens Shares Wife’s Breast Cancer Diagnosis
articles.summary: “Big Brother” Season 28 winner Rick Devens and wife Becca Devens have revealed she was recently diagnosed with breast cancer.
articles.body: “Big Brother” Season 28 winner Rick Devens and wife Becca Devens have revealed she was recently diagnosed with breast cancer. The two shared the news in a joint Instagram video uploaded Oct. 25. “We feel like politicians right now, but we just wanted to let you know some important news because I feel like it’d be weird if we didn’t tell you before I had to go have surgery,” Becca Devens said. “So, Rick won ‘Big Brother.’ And then we came home and I got diagnosed with breast cancer.” Becca Devens continued, “So that sucks. But we caught it early because I do my mammograms like a good girl and I’m going to get a double mastectomy and that’ll be fun.” She said the couple will continue to keep fans updated on her health journey. She added that the next step is to have an MRI on Oct. 27 to confirm the location of the cancer. “If you guys just want to send good vibes and prayers for that, that’s awesome,” she told fans. Rick Devens chimed in and also asked fans to send them love. Becca Devens and her husband said their dog and their two children have been supporting them. “Kids are doing good. Everybody’s OK,” she assured fans. She sarcastically captioned the post “plot twist.” Members of the “Big Brother” and “Survivor” family left uplifting messages, wishing her good health. Rick Devens’ close friend Christian Hubicki, who played with the former news anchor on Season 50 of “Survivor,” wrote, “My best as always to you and your family. You’re the most resilient people I know.” Taylor Brown, who was runner-up on Season 28 of “Big Brother,” said, “Sending love and prayers Ms. Becca.” The official “Big Brother” Instagram account wrote, “We love you mama devens.” Rick Devens expressed his gratitude and left a sweet message for his wife in the comments, too. “Thank you all for the love! Becca’s got this. Luckily she’s the tough one. Also, the funny, charming, smart, good looking one,” he said. Throughout his time in the “Big Brother” house this summer, Rick Devens frequently spoke about how much his wife and their two children mean to him. When he was crowned the winner on Oct. 1, his family immediately joined him on stage, becoming emotional as they celebrated their reunion and his victory. On Oct. 26, Becca Devens provided more details about her diagnosis in another Instagram video. She said she already knew she needed a double mastectomy because in March she had a biopsy on a “little tiny thing” that turned out to be benign. Her latest appointment was a follow-up on the biopsy. “Extensive growth of, I guess, abnormally shaped calcifications and then necrotic tissue were found in my biopsy” she explained. “The type of cancer I have, it is non-invasive. So it’s probably not in my lymph nodes but also they said it’s high grade, which means it grows really fast. And it’s extensively larger than it was in April.” So, she said her doctor “wants it all off.” “And I’m down because my mom had breast cancer and I’m not dealing with that. So if he is going to take lefty, he can take righty too. OK, it’s like a two for one,” she quipped. The point of the MRI, she said, is to confirm the growth hasn’t grown past where her doctor believes it is located. She also shared that she doesn’t have any lumps and the growth is in her duct.
